items.speaker: Hon CLAYTON COSGROVE
items.text: I move, That the House
take note of miscellaneous business . Gerry Brownlee said on Newstalk ZB last week in
respect of the Canterbury ear thquake that people were being impatient. He was right.
The Canterbury earthquake, like the lack of planning and strategy from this
Government, is a very down-to-earth, practical example of the fact that the Government
is a shambles. There is no plan for the peopl e of Canterbury, as there is no plan for the
people of New Zealand.
Let us look at the evidence around th at proposition. Early childhood education
centres around New Zealand are cut to the bone, yet the Minister of Education stands up
day after day as we present example after example—Swannanoa Preschool has received
a $100,000 cut—and says that there is no cut. We have 158,000 New Zealand citizens—
Kiwis—unemployed. One in four young people leaving school is going on the scrap
heap.
Where is the plan around that problem? The only plan articulated by the Government
was the Job Summit. Do members remember that? Then we had a cycleway. Then New
Zealand was to be a financial hub for the world. Then we had the clanger: Gerry
Brownlee, the man who is interested in earth  movements of all kinds, suggested mining
in national parks. I say that the Government ’s programme has more cracks and gaps in
it than the Canterbury earthquake  or a cheap version of the Borat movie. That is what I
say.
16 Feb 2011 General Debate 16825
Gerry Brownlee and the other Ministers get up every day and say that the people are
being impatient and should se ttle down. I say to Mr Br ownlee that the people of
Canterbury are impatient not only for a pl an and a strategy but for any sort of
coordinated, managed effort in respect of their crisis. He should tell his colleagues that
every New Zealander who is unemployed, ev ery mum and dad who is facing a $25 to
$80 a week increase per child in the price of early chil dhood education, and every early
childhood education centre that is facing hundred s of thousands of dollars of cuts, like
the 34 in my patch facing nearly a million dol lars of cuts, are, by God, impatient. They
are impatient for any sort of action.
They are also impatient to know how fa r the asset sales programme that those
members have articulated will take New Z ealand. They are impatient to know that,
given that it was tried last time by that cr ew over there when they were in Government.
They were told that everybody would be bett er off as National flogged off assets willy-
nilly, but they were not. They are impatie nt to know why Nationa l is doing it again.
They are impatient to know why mum and dad Kiwis—according to that crew over
there, benevolent Government that it is—w ill be first in the queue to buy back what
they already own with their own money. Th ey are impatient to know the logic around
that.
The people of New Zealand are impatient to  know how foreign interests that gained
51.8 percent of Contact Energy when it was sold off will be prevented from eventually
gaining our assets. The people of New Zealand are impatient to know where the revenue
streams will come from as the Governme nt flogs off revenue -earning assets. The
Government talks about purchasing non-reve nue earning assets like, for instance,
schools. It is a great thing to build a school; we built heaps of them. But Gerry
Brownlee, as the resident genius, should tell me—and the people of New Zealand are
impatient to know—how a school can genera te revenue as opposed to, say, a State-
owned power company. Many schools, of course, are in the di saster zone of
Christchurch. That man, Gerry Brownlee, stan ds as a stark example, given his lack of
action in respect of the crisis in Canterbury, of the inaction, the shambles, the lack of
planning, and the lack of strategy exhibited across every portfolio in this Government.
I say to Mr Brownlee that he is right : people are being impatient. People are
impatient to know how they will get a j ob, especially the 1 58,000 unemployed Kiwis.
They are impatient to know how they will ge t a job, how they will make ends meet, and
where these mum and dad Kiwis will get this windfall of cash so as to be first in the
queue to buy back assets that they already own. According to National these 158,000
unemployed New Zealanders and others have  tons of dough! They are impatient, they
want a job, they want action, and they want a plan. I say to Mr Brownlee that he should
try to deliver one.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: First, I would like to take a
moment to extend my sympathies to the fam ily of Private Mila and the other families
involved in the incident in Af ghanistan. Private Mila will be sorely missed, and I wish
those injured the speediest recovery possible.
Today is a special day in the Australia - New Zealand relationship. Australia and
New Zealand have one of the most open ec onomic and trade relatio nships of any two
countries. Australia has a population that is five times the size of  New Zealand’s, and
the thing that should give pause for thought to every member in this Chamber is the fact
that the Australian economy is seven tim es the size of New Zealand’s economy.
Australia is the most important trading part ner we have, and it is New Zealand’s closest
neighbour.
It was a real pleasu
re to hear the Australia n Prime Minister speak in this House this
morning. It was also pleasing to  hear her observe, as have almost all Australian Prime
16826 General Debate 16 Feb 2011
Ministers before her, the importance of Australia being an open economy, and the
recognition of the importance of the economic reforms of the 1980s and 1990s—painful
though they were for both countries—in giving Australia the prosperity that it enjoys
today. Indeed, the enduring consensus on ec onomic policy in Aust ralia is undoubtedly
one of the strong reasons for its continued economic success.
I have to say that that contrasts with some  of the economic debate  that this country
sticks itself with from time to time. Here, what describes itself as the fraternal party of
the Australian Labor Party seems to be st arting to advocate 1970s-style, Fortress New
Zealand policies as some way of attaini ng economic nirvana. Th at is undoubtedly not
correct.
Australia knows that a lot is to be gained  by encouraging foreign investment. It has
the economy and the income to show for it. Therefore, the easier we can make it for
companies to operate in both countries by removing unnecessary barriers, the greater
the opportunities for business to have conf idence, to make substantial productivity
gains, and to take up new opportunities that will help to underpin growth and jobs. That
is, incidentally, something the former trade Minister Phil Goff used to believe in and
work towards. Now, sadly, in this House in the last 2 weeks he has been using
xenophobia to make cheap political points about German and Australian investors, just
as the previous speaker did in this general debate today.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I take offence at the
accusation that members on this side of th e House have been using xenophobia. Some
of us find that accusation deeply offensive.

items.speaker: Chris Tremain
items.text: Surely this is a debating point, and not one that the member should
take offence to. To call a member xenophobic is hardly a criminal offence in this House.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Mr Speaker—

items.speaker: Mr SPEAKER
items.text: I do not want to take any more time on this. I will ask the member
to withdraw the comment, but I do not want to be too pedantic about ruling out words;
we can all take offence at all sorts of th ings. Members must be very careful not to
accuse another member of being racist, and I guess one could claim there is a
connotation here. So I ask the member to withdraw, but I will not rule out words forever
because offence might have been taken on one occasion. If the honourable member
would withdraw that word please.

items.speaker: Hon STEVEN JOYCE
items.text: I withdraw, and say that the member is now using criticism
of German investors and criticism of Australi an investors a number of times, as did the
previous speaker in this House.
Today a very important investment protoc ol was signed between our two countries,
which sets a higher threshold for trans-Tasman investment so that it does not have to go
through a screening process. This will do much for the confidence of New Zealand
businesses growing in Australi a, and in the two countries , where they will have a
combined domestic market in the order of 25 million people. It is this sort of work that
will help New Zealand companies to grow, th at will create jobs, and that will give
companies the opportunity to create a stronger economy in New Zealand.
It is interesting that th is should occur on a day like today, when Fletcher’s, our
largest listed company, which is very active in Australia, has recorded an improved
result. It just goes to show the potentia l of strong economic gr owth and a tighter
economic market between our two countries. That is what this House should be
focusing on. The opportunity today is to focus on that, because we need this country to
grow much more strongly, and working closely with Australia will allow us to do so. I
salute the investment protocol that was signed by our two Prime Ministers today.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: It is interesting to follow
on from Steven Joyce. I just note for the record that Phil Goff, as trade Minister for New
16 Feb 2011 General Debate 16827
Zealand, helped to create hundreds, if not  thousands, of jobs by signing free-trade
agreements, and negotiating free-t rade agreements like the one with China. That is far
more than that hollow man over there will ever do. He can stand up in this House and
crow about his focus groups and what he learns from them, but the real work of being in
Government, of being a trade Minister like Ph il Goff was, of actually helping to create
jobs, is not what that Minister is doing. He is part of a Government that has overseen
158,000 people being unemployed—158,000. That is  what he has overseen. Once again
from Steven Joyce we have heard the theme of this Government: that someone else is to
blame.
There is always someone else to blame. Today the Prime Minister stood in the House
and said beneficiaries were to blame. They were making a lifestyle choice; that is what
the Prime Minister said today. The three wome n who came to the electorate clinic that I
held in Wellington Central on Saturday, who were all in their 40s or 50s, all out of
work, all desperate to get a job, and all trying to redevelop their skills to get a job, are
wondering what the Government is doing for them. They want to know what the
Government is doing for them, to help to cr eate jobs for them. But no, Mr Key stood in
the House today and said they were to blame for being unemployed and they were
making a lifestyle choice. I say it is not a lif estyle choice for those people, and Mr Key
would know that if he actually talked to people on the ground.
But Mr Key himself has come up with something else today, for which someone else
is to blame. This is the purchase of the BMWs. The story has moved on three times
today. Firstly, it was Labour’s fault, because it had locked the Government into a
contract whereby it had to purchase a new set of BMWs. Of course, that turned out not
to be the case. In fact, it was an option to renew the contract , so it was not the case that
Labour had locked the Government into a contract. The Prime Minister moved on and
said it was the Greens’ fault, when actually it was Bill English’s. But the Prime Minister
moved on and said it was the Greens’ fault, because they were interested in a fad called
lowering carbon emissions. Apparently, the fl eet of BMWs was to have lower carbon
emissions. Apparently lowe ring carbon emissions, doing  something about climate
change, is a fad, so it is the Greens’ fault.
But then the third story was that it was th e fault of the Department of Internal
Affairs. Apparently, Mr Key is “furious” with the Depart ment of Internal Affairs,
except that that is fudging the story a bit, b ecause the part of the department that is
responsible for the purchasing of those cars is Ministerial Services.

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: He should read the papers.

items.speaker: GRANT ROBERTSON
items.text: Who is the Minister responsib le for Ministerial Services?
That would be the Prime Minister. So in actual fact if Mr Key is blaming the department
he is blaming Ministerial Services, and he is the Minister responsible for Ministerial
Services. As Mr Mallard said, Mr Key is clearly not reading his papers. If the Prime
Minister wants to take some responsibility for this fiasco, it is in his basket. He is the
Minister responsible for Mi nisterial Services. He cannot blame the department, he
cannot blame Labour, and he cannot blame the Green Party.
That is the problem with this Governme nt. Although it has no plan, there is always
someone else to blame. It is not good enough. The State sector is being fingered as the
area to blame, because apparent ly it is bloated and inefficient. Yet Standard and Poor’s
has said today it does not regard the State sector in New Zealand as being bloated and
inefficient. Kyran Curry, its analyst, said in the New Zealand Herald today: “Generally,
we look at the Government in New Zealand as  being relatively small and compared to
its peers it’s quite efficient.” That is right . Standard and Poor’s, the rating agency that
the Government puts so much investment in, says that actually it  does not do anything.
16828 General Debate 16 Feb 2011
The State sector is not bloated and ineffici ent. But once again from this Government
there is always somebody else to blame.
We saw that again today from Anne Tolley on early childhood education. Once again
the increase in fees is the fault of the kindergartens and the early childhood centres, or it
is the fault of the parents. But it is not. It is the fault of this Government for taking
money out of a vital sector. Once again, the G overnment says someone else is to blame.
Anne Tolley says she is not to blame for taking money out of the sector; it is the
centres’ fault for putting up their fees. It is not . It is the fault of this Government, which
has absolutely no plan for th is country to grow the econom y and no plan for jobs. Once
again, Government members stand in the Hous e and try to find someone else to blame.
It is time for this Government to look in the mirror.

items.speaker: CRAIG FOSS
items.text: This is a sad day for our nation. It is also a
day of celebration, of firsts, and of gr eatness. Let me acknowledge a fallen New
Zealand soldier overseas. I join others in the House and the vari ous party leaders who
made speeches earlier. This is a sad, sad moment. But it is also a day of celebration and
firsts. It was an honour and a pleasure to hear the Austra lian Prime Minister, Julia
Gillard, speak to the House.
Today was the first time a leader of a foreign Government has spoken to the House—
using the word “foreign” and the word “Aus tralia” just does not seem to work—and it
was a pleasure to hear the way she delivered  her speech, the conten t of the speech, and
her acknowledgment of the real ities of the position of bot h our countries. Sure, New
Zealand is small and Australia is much larger , but that presents opportunities to both of
our countries. We acknowledge our shared past, our shared whakapapa, if you like, in
many, many of the historic moments around our country.
However, I must say “Open the Gate, Mat e”. That was the catchcry of the Aussie
apple protests that began in 2005 and picked up on 90-odd years of protests before that.
The angle was not particularly acknowledge d. Hawke’s Bay is a large apple-producing
area, as are Nelson, Otago, and areas of the Wa irarapa, etc. The apple industry is a very
large industry for New Zealand. It employs many low-skilled people, and, of course,
some higher-skilled people along the way. The point is that New Ze aland apples could
not get into Australia.
I will not relitigate the various debates, as I think members know them very well, but
I acknowledge the Australian Apple Access Gro up from the Hawke’s Bay that, with its
partners in Nelson, got the momentum and the ball rolling again. I still recall jumping
on the steam train to come down to Welli ngton from the Hawke’s Bay, to march on
Parliament in May 2005. Good friends of people in Hawke’s Bay got the message to the
Government of the time to start some action. Some action did start to happen, to be fair.
Attention came to the issue and to the inhere nt unfairness of it. The gate is now open,
mate.
I acknowledge fully Prime Minister Gillard’s comments in the House and elsewhere
about the issue. I w ould like to q uote the headline from the Australian newspaper,
which reported on the Australian Prime Minist er’s speech, because it captures it all:
“PM applauded as she declares apple war truce in historic speech to New Zealand
MPs”. We have to look forward. The agreement creates huge opportunities for the apple
industry and for New Zealand.
The investment protocol, whic h the Hon Steven Joyce was just talking about, brings
the opportunities of a 25 milli on purchaser-consumer market on the doorstep of New
Zealand, and another of our primary produc ts will now be accessible over there,
probably by next season, with a bit of luck.
The point is
that it is not a fight; it is a partnership. It is about  seizing the moment
and seizing the opportunity. The global umpire of world trade, the World Trade
16 Feb 2011 General Debate 16829
Organization, has made a ruling and the Aust ralians have accepted it, and now we are
both working hand in hand to seize the opportuniti es of the moment. Parallel to that is
the investment protocol, and th e work that Simon Power is continuing. As the Minister
of Finance acknowledged earlier today, much of the work was begun under the previous
administration. We freely acknowledge that f act, although it does raise the question as
to why various other speeches made by the Leader of the Opposition seem to be
contradictory. Some time back, Mr Goff esse ntially said he woul d renegotiate CER, I
think, and here we are today celebrating a growth of CER.
Anyone who ever doubts the worth of CER to New Zealand and to all of Australasia
should imagine New Zealand without CER. Imagine how many jobs would be lost,
where our interest rates would be, and how  vulnerable our finan ce sector would be,
particularly following recent events. Today is a celebration of our mateship and
comradeship with our good friends and colleagues in Australia. As both Prime Ministers
alluded to, we are almost family.
I look forward to our Australian friends and family enjoying New Zealand apples,
alongside New Zealand wine, and I look forward to welcoming them as we continue our
discussions and negotiations towards having one open domestic airl ine market, if, in
fact, we can get there. The goodwill shown by both leaders today—and across the
House, to be fair—points towards a very positive future indeed. Thank you, on this very
great day of celebration.

items.speaker: JACINDA ARDERN
items.text: This week it has all unravelled for the
Government. This week we have seen that all the eggs the Government had in terms of
an unemployment plan not only were few but also were broken. In the face of
unemployment at 6.8 percent, which repr esents 158,000 people, the Labour Opposition
demanded from the Government a plan. In deed, the 158,000 people in the dole queue
demanded a plan. The 52,000 people who have jo ined that queue since the Government
came into office demanded a plan. The one  in four young people—the school-leavers,
who have not even had a chance to enter th e workforce—being left on the scrap heap
because there are no jobs demanded a pl an. We cannot forget the 12 percent of
unemployed 20 to 24-year-olds, which represents a good chunk of young graduates who
have left university with skills that they  are willing and wanting to use. They also
demanded a plan because they, too, are waiting for work.
What did we get in the face of those de mands? First came the excuses. Every time
the unemployment figures came out and shocked the Government just a little by
increasing, the Government claimed that figu res tend to be volatile and to move around
a bit. Second, the Minister for Social De velopment and Employment, Paula Bennett,
who is AWOL currently, claimed that the une mployed just needed to take a positive
attitude if they wanted to find work. Toda y we heard the Prime Minister claim that
some people on the benefit are making a lifestyl e choice in the way they exist. Finally,
at some point in the debate we heard the Government acknowledge the real issue that
was at play: Kiwis want work, but there are no jobs—there are no jobs. That is the real
reason that 158,000 Kiwis are currently seeking work.
It is time that, instead of making excuses,  the Government starts doing something
about it. Our expectation was that after 2 ye ars there would be a plan. What have we
seen instead? We have seen a series of gimmicks. I do not use that turn of phrase
lightly. At first, there may have been some  hope that something concrete could come
out something like the Job Summit. We also saw the cycleway idea. I am the first to
acknowledge that I do not have a problem with  the concept of a cycleway. In and of
itself, I think it is a positive thing, but it w ould never have been the answer, and it has
proven not to be the answer, to a growing unemployment issue in New Zealand. In fact,
16830 General Debate 16 Feb 2011
we have seen a grand total of 214 jobs created out of the cycleway. It is just not good
enough.
What was the other option the Government gave to us? It was a youth unemployment
package: Job Ops and Community Max. Th e New Zealand Institute of Economic
Research told us that the Government deserved a C on that package. Why? Because it
would at best assist 8 percent of young unemployed people.
What have we seen for the 8 percent of young unemployed people who have had
some contact with those schemes? Well, let us look at Community Max. Work and
Income claimed it would be a chance to up skill young people and move them into jobs.
At a cost of $100 million in total for J ob Ops and Community Max, I would have
thought we could expect that at the very least. But when we scratch the surface, what do
we see? Some projects have delivered what it was claimed they would deliver; others
have proven to be a dismal failure. If this was indeed a chance to upskill our young
people, why was Work and Income not check ing that the subsidy it was giving to
providers to train people was being appr opriately used? The general public would
expect that, if we are spending $18,000 to put  fewer than six people into a job where
text messages are being sent, we would s ee some outcomes. What  skills is a young
person getting for a future career by sendi ng text messages all day to defendants,
reminding them of court appearances? Absolutely none. If we are to spend over
$300,000 on a gardening project, we should at least upskill the young people who are in
that project. Instead, we see half of them without jobs at the end of it.
The Government has claimed that 70 percent of people on Community Max have not
presented at Work and Income again or gone on to main benefits again. That is an
absolute distortion of the truth. Seventy pe rcent of people have not walked through the
Work and Income door again, but that does not mean they are employed. We know that
40,000 young people in New Zealand are not in employment, education, or training.
Community Max participants have joined that dismal number. Where is the plan?

items.speaker: KATRINA SHANKS
items.text: Firstly, I offer my condolences on the loss of the
New Zealand soldier Private Kirifi Mila. My thoughts and prayers are with the soldier’s
family and friends today and for the next weeks, which will be hard for them.
I would like to respond quickly to the Wellington Central member of Parliament,
Grant Robertson, who earlier in  this debate said that Na tional did nothing for growth
and to get New Zealand ahead. When filming of The Hobbit  in Wellington was at risk,
we did not hear a word from that member. He was silent on what was happening with
The Hobbit. If he is really serious about gettin g some industry into Wellington he has to
stand up and back what is happening within Wellington, and The Hobbit is absolutely
crucial to Wellington and to keeping Peter Jackson in Wellington.
Today we saw a part of history. Today th e forty-ninth Parliament of New Zealand
had the privilege to witness the first address by any foreign leader in our House of
Representatives. Today New Zealanders from around the country were able to watch
live as the Prime Minister of Australia, th e Hon Julia Gillard, spoke in this very
debating chamber. Australia and New Zealand were together in our debating chamber;
we are two nations whose histories are inna tely entwined, and today we became two
nations whose futures together are boundl ess. Today history was made, and the
National-led Government’s vision for an even closer friendship, relationship, and union
with Australia was born. The ongoing devel opment of a trans-Tasman single economic
market and a seamless operating environment for Australian and New Zealand
businesses are the ends that our Government is working towards, and today that was the
vision Prime Minister Gillard committed to. The relationship between New Zealand and
Australia has always been one of great importance to us.
16 Feb 2011 General Debate 16831
In her speech the Prime Minister said that  Australia and New Zealand were island
nations that nobody owed a living; if we gain ed any advantage in the world, it would be
because we fought for it and earned it. To day, as our Prime Minister signed the
Investment Protocol to th e Australia and New Zealand Closer Economic Relations
Trade Agreement, the National-led Governme nt achieved a milestone fundamental to
that fight. Enhanced economic relations be tween our two nations are fundamental to
National’s goal of a single economic mark et for our nations. For over 30 years New
Zealand and Australia have pur sued greater economic integration and partnership. We
believe that a strong economic relationship be tween our two countries will benefit both
of us. Julia Gillard talked in her speech  about the cross-pollination of ideas and
innovations between our nations, and in par ticular between our countries’ business
sectors. She said that we w ould be able to share the weal th of knowledge in businesses.
We would be able to learn and we would be  great. As we work ed towards the common
goal of a single economic market, our economies would be able to complement each
other with our strengths, and pull each other up from our weaknesses.
At the end of last year I attended the HER Wellington Businesswoman of the Year
Awards. There were fresh ideas, innovation, and recipients who through their hard work
and passion were leading the way in thei r fields. The winner of the supreme award,
Camilla Welch, owner and general manager of  a label-making and printing business in
Pētone, was selected for her personal drive and business sense. She proved that business
excellence and environmenta l friendliness can be mutu ally rewarding. Tourism,
agriculture, film—N ew Zealand has the knowledge to lead the world in many fields.
But as John Powell once wrote, the only real  mistake is the one from which we learn
nothing. The easier we make it for companie s to operate in both New Zealand and
Australia, the more we will learn and the greater the opportunities for business will be.
Refreshing ideas, innovation, and expertise underpin long-term business growth in New
Zealand, and underpin a strong economy for our country.
Like most New Zealanders, I have experienced firsthand how the unique relationship
between our nations allows Kiwis and Aussies  to lead successful lives in each other’s
countries. For the past 25 years my sister ha s lived and worked in Australia. At any
other time in history taking my family to visi t her or for her to visit me could have been
a completely different story. But today it ha s never been easier. We visit each other
continually, back and forth ac ross the Ditch. Australia is our closest ally, and the idea
that people can move, work, and live across the Ditch is often taken for granted by New
Zealanders. People in many countries cannot do this with the ease we ourselves do it.
For business and investors to enjoy such  a seamless transition is a goal of our
Government. As Prime Minister Gillard stood in front of our  colleagues today, she said
that New Zealand might be a small nation, but  we were one with a bold vision of its
place in this world.

items.speaker: HILARY CALVERT
items.text: Earlier today we saw a rare show of respect in this
House between the people of New Zealand and our closest neighbour. But where is the
respect from this House when it comes to allowing the people of New Zealand the
chance to have their say?
This House will soon be debating the Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Bill.
The way this bill has been dealt with to date  is a travesty of justice. It shows why the
public has lost its respect for politicians. In 2004 the Labour Government took away the
rights of Mā ori to go to court. The h īkoi that concluded outside  th is Chamber was the
largest New Zealand has ever seen. The opposition to that bill, from Mā ori and non-
Māori alike, spelt the end of that Labour Government. The Marine and Coastal Area
(Takutai Moana) Bill continues the injustice, and the nation has again mobilised against
it. Submissions to the M āori Affairs Committee on the bill were overwhelmingly
16832 General Debate 16 Feb 2011
negative; 5,000 written submissions and 500 oral  submissions left the committee in no
doubt that this bill is fatally flawed. The committee’s response was to shut down debate,
and it surprised this House by reporting b ack early. The committee recommended no
changes to the bill, yet the Minister in char ge of the bill has clearly indicated that
changes need to be made. Officials recommended that 89 of the 124 clauses in the bill
be changed. They recommended an average of four changes per clause—a total of more
than 380 changes. The bill was reported back to the House with none of those more than
380 changes. As the bill stands, it will still allow for backroom po litical deals without
public scrutiny. It will still not clearly spell out  that access to the foreshore and seabed
will remain free. It will not respect any of  the submitters who gave up their time to
participate in a democratic process.
This is the House of Representatives, and in it we need to respect people. The people
put us here, and the people decide when we leave. That is democracy; we disrespect it at
our peril. The Attorney-General has promised that he will seek to make changes through
Supplementary Order Papers. Those Supplementa ry Order Papers will  be presented to
us without notice at the Committee stage. Backroom deals, hasty changes, and improper
process are not the hallmarks of a respectful relationship. We woul d not be accused of
treating our neighbouring countries this way, and we should not treat our own people
this way.

items.speaker: PHIL TWYFORD
items.text: The people are waiting for a plan. They are waiting
for this Government to come up with some thing concrete, something realistic, about
youth unemployment. They are waiting for an  acknowledgment that, particularly in
Auckland, there is a housing crisis, but it does not appear, from the Prime Minister’s
comments in question time today, that he ev en accepts there is a problem. They are
waiting to hear when this Government will do something about the number of
apprentices that are being laid off. They want to know when this Government will come
up with a plan to grow the economy and get us out of this mess.
But while people are waiting for a plan, the people in Auckland over recent weeks
have been handed a fiasco and a shambles. We  have seen that shambles in the creation
of the M āori Statutory Board on the Auckland Counc il, put in place by this National
Government. The board w ill appoint unelected M āori members to council committees,
where much of the work of council is done, and those members will be given full voting
rights. That is an abuse of democratic principles. What is worse is that the M āori
Statutory Board, according to the most r ecent estimates, will end up costing the
Auckland ratepayer up to $1.9 million a year. Th at is an outrage, and Aucklanders are
angry. They do not understand why the Government has done that. They are being hit in
the pocket to fund that undemocratic Māori Statutory Board.
Let us recount a bit of the story that w ill explain how we got there. Back in 2009
Rodney Hide threatened to resign at the prospect of dedicated M āori seats on the
Auckland Council. Unfortunately, the Prime Minister did not accept that offer. The
Prime Minister did a shabby deal with the M āori Party to instead insert a M āori
Statutory Board into the Auckland Council.  He bypassed a perfectly good proposal for
democratically elected M āori seats on the Auckland Council , and instead put unelected
people there. Then, at the behest of the M āori Pa rty at the select committee, a deal was
done—a shabby deal—to give the members of  those council committees, appointed by
the unelected M āori Statutory Board, full voting right s alongside councillors who had
been elected by the people of Auckland. Th at is an outrage. The columns of the New
Zealand Herald are full of it, and Aucklanders do not like it.
I see that TV3 has just launched a new satire series. It is a comedy series designed to
send up Rodney Hide’s super-city. But TV3 do es not need to make a comedy, and it
does not need to make a satire; it should just come here and listen to Rodney Hide in
16 Feb 2011 General Debate 16833
this House, because nobody could write this stuff. This is the self-styled “Minister for
Ratepayers”. He is the fallen perk-buster.  Yet what has he done? He has stiffed the
Auckland ratepayer for $1.9 million a year to f und his statutory board. He claims to be
the great apostle of the one person, one vot e principle. He claims to be the great
champion of democracy. Yet what has he done? He has imposed on the people of
Auckland an unelected board with decisi on-making powers as members of council
committees. That is wrong.
There is a reason Aucklanders do not like it, and we have heard over the last few
days some interesting voices. Mike Lee, the former chairman of the Auckland Regional
Council, has called this an appalling fiasco. He  has said that Key and Hide should fix it.
What has Cameron Brewer said? Cameron Brew er is not exactly a leading light of the
left on the Auckland Council. What has he said? He has said that the Auckland Council
has been let down by poorly drafted legislation. Mayor Len Brown is trying to make the
best of a bad deal. He is trying to work w ith the statutory board and abide by the terms
of the legislation. What is Pita Sharples, the Minister of M āori Affairs, and Rodney
Hide’s ministerial colleague, saying? He is saying that Rodney Hide should either stand
by his legislation or resign.
But we saw in the House today that Rodne y Hide has no inten tion of resigning.
Rodney Hide has refused to take responsibility for th is mess and this fiasco. It is in his
DNA. We have seen it before in the House. We saw it when he t ook his girlfriend on a
trip to London, Toronto, Portla nd, and Los Angeles, and sp ent tens of thousands of
dollars of taxpayers’ money. There was a week of news interviews, door-stopping in the
corridors of Parliament, and embarrassing revelations, before Rodney Hide finally
backed down, took responsibility, and paid back some of that money. We saw it with
his withholding of information for years a bout David Garrett, the ACT Party’s former
law and order spokesperson.

items.speaker: PESETA SAM LOTU-IIGA
items.text: It is a pleasure and an
honour to speak today. Today is a historic day for the House of Representatives of New
Zealand. As has already been noted by other speakers, the Prime Minister of Australia is
the first world leader to address this Parlia ment, albeit outside sitting times. It was an
honour to hear her words of encouragement. It was an honour to hear what having a
relationship with New Zealand means for her and her country.
Australia is our closest ally. She spoke  about Australia and New Zealand being
family. She spoke of the history that was forged on the battlegrounds of Gallipoli and
around the world. Of course, the history was also forged in our similar cultures—in the
culture we share with Australians—and on the sports battlegrounds.
Today is a day of celebration, but it is also  a day of sadness. We heard that another
member of the New Zealand Defence Force sadly lost his life overnight. It is a sad day
when we lose defence people in foreign lands, but we salute Private Kirifi Mila for his
service to this country, and we certainly salute him for the service he gave to democracy
and freedom around the world.
We heard today that the partnership—C loser Economic Relations—between New
Zealand and Australia has been enhanced. It has been enhanced through an investment
protocol. The investment protocol is critical, because as we climb out of the global
economic recession, it is important that i nvestment continues to flow to our New
Zealand businesses. When I visit the busines ses in the Maungakiekie electorate—
spanning from Onehunga in the west to M ount Wellington, Penrose, and Panmure, the
heartland of manufacturing and industry in Auckland—they say that the keys to their
success will be the upskilling of people but also access to capital. The investment
protocol for New Zealand and Australia ensu res that more funds will flow to those
16834 General Debate 16 Feb 2011
businesses and that there will be more inve stment opportunities and more jobs and food
for our people and for New Zealanders around the country.
The protocol is more than an economic agreement, as we have heard from the Prime
Ministers of both New Zealand and Australia. We heard from Ms Gillard that it is about
highly mobile and educated populations. It is  about having capable and effective armed
forces harnessed in partnership. We have co mmitted to working with the Australians in
a range of different areas, including defen ce. Our own Prime Minister, the Rt Hon John
Key, referred to Australians and New Zealanders establishing friendships and leading
successful lives in each other’s countries. Having lived in Australia and having forged a
number of close relationships with Australian people, I concur with our Prime Minister.
I will share with members a little story. Over  the Christmas break I visited Australia.
I visited a friend of my mine, a brother, and someone I consider to be a family member.
He is suffering from cancer. [ Interruption] If Mr Twyford thinks it is funny for me to
tell a personal story then I feel sorry for him. I visited my friend. I have known the
bloke for over 15 years. He is married to a New Zealander. He has a New Zealand -
Australian child. I consider him a brother. Our passion for our families, for sport, for
business, and for the Australian and New Zealan d way brings us toge ther as friends but
also as brothers. I wish him well: Mark Robert Copping.
Finally, I will make a statement in Samoan a bout our fallen soldie r. Ua vala’auina e
le Atua le uso le Susuga a Kirifi Mila. E momoli atu ai o matou alofa’aga ma tatalo mo
le ’aiga fa’anoanoa. Ia pa’i atu le ’a’ao fa’amafanafana o le Atua. Ia manuia ma maua le
filemu. Soifua. Thank you.

items.speaker: SUE KEDGLEY
items.text: The Green Party welcomes the enduring friendship
between Australia and New Zealand. We were pleased to have the Prime Minister of
Australia, Julia Gillard, address our Parliament in a special session in a way that did not
undermine a long-held parliamentary convention. It is interesting that because of the
same parliamentary convention we will not allow the Queen or the Governor-General to
address our Parliament in the Chamber when it is in session, yet most parties were only
too eager to abandon the convention for the sake of Julia Gillard.
It is also interesting that many members of the House have waxed eloquent about the
warmth of our relationship with Australia and about how much we respect and admire
Australians, yet in the same Chamber our co -leader Dr Russel Norman is subjected to
constant abuse by many members of the House, particular by those on the National side,
simply because he is an Australian. I do not hear members shouting abuse at members
who originate from England, India, or Sri Lanka , but it is almost as though it is a sin or
a crime for Dr Norman to be an Australian. He has to tolerate that level of abuse in the
House. What does it say about our real respect  for Australians? I learnt from the Prime
Minister of Australia that one of our fore most Prime Ministers, Michael Joseph Savage,
was an Australian. I wonder whether he too was subjected to similar abuse for the crime
of being an Australian.
The Green Party strongly supports building closer relations with our kith and kin
across the Tasman. I doubt whether any politicians in the House have closer relations
than we do with Green MPs in Australia. We have joint sessions and we have made
joint submissions to Food Standards Australia New Zealand, so we are very committed
to having strong political and other ties with  Australia. We acknowledge that we have
more special ties with Australia than we  do with any other nation, but we want our
relationship with Australia to be a partne rship between two equal nations. We do not
want to become, effectively, the seventh state of Australia, or a country that is more and
more controlled and dominated by Australia.
Already, most of our banks and many of our key institutions are owned by Australian
businesses. The agreement today for further investment liberalisation will speed up that
16 Feb 2011 General Debate 16835
process. Lifting the threshold for Australian foreign investment that does not require
any regulatory approval or scrutiny from our Overseas I nvestment Office will simply
mean that more and more of our companies— and, of course, any future assets that the
National Government puts up for sale—wi ll end up in Australian ownership. The
Government’s pledge that New Zealand investors will get the first crack at buying
shares in any future sell-off of State-owned assets is simply a hollow pledge—pure spin,
really—because everyone knows that there is no way to prevent those shares from being
sold offshore after a certain date. So on a day when we welcomed the Prime Minister of
Australia into our Chamber, I think it is appropriate that we reflect on our growing
political as well as economic subservience to Australia.
Some may sneer at that statement, but the truth is that we have already forged one
relationship—the treaty that set up Food Standards Australia New Zealand—whereby
we are completely subservient to Australia a nd we have the same status as Tasmania. A
previous National Government signed up to a deal in the mid-1990s whereby we ceded
our sovereignty over food labe lling and composition to Food Standards Australia New
Zealand. That organisation is based in Canberra, was set up under Australian legislation,
and is chaired by an Australian Minister for Health and Ageing and serviced by an
Australian ministry. We have one vote out of 11 on the governing council—I repeat;
one vote out of 11. That is hard to believe, a nd when I point that out to New Zealanders
they are outraged by it.
The problem with our membership of Food Standards Australia New Zealand is not
just that it is dominated by Australia and we  have one vote out of 11 but that, in joining
up with Food Standards Australia New Z ealand, we gave up our jurisdiction—the
jurisdiction of this Parliame nt—over all of the issues that we ceded to that body. We
cannot pass laws in this House about food labelling or food composition. I discovered
that when I introduced my C onsumer’s Right to Know (Food Information) Bill. I went
to the Clerk, who said I could not say Pa rliament should introduc e GE labelling or
mandatory country-of-origin labelling. The Clerk said our Parliament has no jurisdiction
over these matters. We have ceded that to the Australian-based body, where we have
one vote out of 11.

items.speaker: AARON GILMORE
items.text: I will carry on from what Sue Kedgley, the
previous speaker, was saying. I will talk a little about the brot herhood of men and
women in Australia and New Zealand, and I will touch on one aspect the previous
speaker mentioned. It is not the case that we do not like Russel Norman because he is an
Australian; we just do not like his politics.
I will talk about some of the things that link my family to Australia. Some members
may know what is on the A$10 note. If member s ever have an A$10 note, they should
pull it out and look at it one day. On the A$10 not e is one of the most famous socialists
in Australia we could ever have met, Dame Mary Gilmore. Dame Mary Gilmore was a
journalist, a literary writer fo r many years, and a poet in Au stralia. She was one of the
most famous journalists and writers in Australia, and she was a very well-known
socialist with the Australian Workers’ Union, as I am sure some members opposite
know. One of the neat things a bout her being on the A$10 note is that it shows us some
of the links between our coun try and Australia that are to  do with aspects other than
those we have traditionally talked about relating to sport and our defence forces.
I will talk p
articularly about some of the changes that have been signed off today.
Those changes are in the field of business. One of  the things that have been announced
today is that New Zealand businesses will be ab le to invest up to $1 billion in Australia.
There has been a lot of worry and concern about Australian companies investing in New
Zealand, but having New Zealand companies bei ng able to invest up  to $1 billion in
Australia is a very good thi ng. I will give members a coupl e of examples. Right now a
16836 General Debate 16 Feb 2011
very large New Zealand company in the bu ilding products area is in the process of
taking over a very large Australian compa ny. That transaction is worth about $700
million or $800 million. Ordinarily, such a transaction, in a simple sense, would require
some sort of approvals, but with the signing of the protocols today, such transactions do
not need such bureaucratic approvals and can go ahead in a more efficient manner. That
is a classic example of the benefits of Cl oser Economic Relations and the extension of
the protocols between our two great nations.
We heard Jacinda Ardern talk ing earlier about some of th e issues around skills. She
said she was worried about wasted skills in  terms of teaching people how to use text
messages in jobs. Well, I ask whether th at member wants ev erybody to sit on a
production line doing nothing an d learning nothing for the rest  of their lives. Teaching
young people skills is one way of getting them better, higher-paid, and more productive
jobs, which is what our Government is about.
We heard Clayton Cosgrove bleating about earthquakes and talk ing about worries
arising from earthquakes. Well, one of the great things about the links between New
Zealand and Australia mentioned today by Prim e Minister Gillard is  the fact that down
in Canterbury, where I live, many Australians are helping to rebuild our houses. They
are helping to inspect houses and are providi ng us with skills we did not have. We did
not have sufficient skills and expertise in Canterbury immediately after the earthquake.
Australia did, and many Australians have been busy working and helping with the
planning and rebuilding for Canterbury. That is a wonderful step forward.
At Pike River on the West Coast, Austra lians have been providing many resources
and skills. That is a wonderf ul example of the joint nature of Australia and New
Zealand. The fact that Australians came over and provided us with resources that we did
not have access to shows the wonderful natu re of the link between Australia and New
Zealand.
Of course, there are also wonderful things to do with sport—in particular, the wider
aspects of sport. Sport is a very global business these days, and the ability to buy, trade,
and sell professional sports teams is increasi ngly part of the nature of the world of
business transactions. Russell Crowe, a Kiwi whom we lent to Australia and of whom
we are probably proud, is a major owner of  the South Sydney Rabbitohs. It will be
possible to buy into other major sporting franchises that are likely to appear.
Over time we are likely to see more and more examples of Australian and New
Zealand businesses becoming in creasingly intertwined. More j obs and expertise will be
created, and trade between the two countries, which is currently something in the order
of $21 billion, will be able to grow. It has been at over 8 percent per annum over the last
decade, and it will continue to grow after the signing of the Closer Economic Relations
protocol.
We have heard fear and loathing from Opposition members about having Australians
coming to invest in New Zealand. Well, I ask them what is wrong with Australians
bringing expertise and skills into New Zealand. What is wrong with that? Australians
bring new skills and wealth into our country, which helps to employ New Zealanders.
That is a good thing. Having productive jobs and investment is a positive thing. We did
not hear that from Ms Ardern earlier on. She did not think training made a lot of sense.
For her, training people in new skills seemed to be a complete waste of time.
Finally, I say to the Australians out there th at we like them, but we do not love them.
I deal with a lot of them, and increasingly the ones I meet when I am travelling round
the world—

items.speaker: Hon Shane Jones
items.text: “I’ve been everywhere, man.”
AARON GI

items.speaker: LMORE
items.text: Shane Jones has been everywhe re, man. Mr Jones is a classic
example of one of the Australians who has done well.
16 Feb 2011 General Debate 16837

items.speaker: Hon SHANE JONES
items.text: Kia ora anō tātou. Tēnā koe, Mr Assistant Speaker
Roy. I have been told there are 40 weeks left until the day that the National Party and its
discredited friends come over to this side of  the House into Opposition. It will not be a
clean transition. The most recent speaker, Mr Gi lmore, will not be a part of that group.
The No. 1 reason is that he will disappear, like the much-vaunted assets he skites about,
when he stands in Christchurch—because there is no place for him on the list. We know
that in order for the scint illating intellect of Mr Paul  Quinn to be preserved and
projected forward, Aaron Gilmore has to go. Th at is a small but largely irrelevant piece
of information.
I come back to Mr Hide. Rodney Hide is the man who threatened to resign. He is the
man who said he would not be blackmailed into resigning if M āori became members of
the super-city council. Today we have  seen dodging, hiding, concealing, and
camouflaging. That has been the style of operation from Rodney Hide. He introduced
legislation reforming, altering, and adjusti ng the structures around the Auckland City
Council and did not vote against the inclusion of a M āori Statutory Board, a board that
has turned into a fiasco. That board is cos ting a great deal of money—too much money,
it would appear to the Auckland ratepayers.
I ask who is responsible. Not Mr Hide! I ask at what point Rodney Hide will explain
to the ratepayers that he is responsible fo r the increase in their rates in Epsom, or
explain to Auckland ratepayers or his electors how Dr Pita Sharples outsmarted him.
That may seem both a physical and an intell ectual impossibility, but the reality is that
the person with bragging rights  here is Dr Pita Sharples , despite his having suffered
considerable public injury for being ineffectual and for not bringing forward what ought
to have happened to elected M āori representatives on the s uper-city. Taihoa, I say to
whānau in Tāmaki-makau-rau—help is on the way!
The Prime Minister said after the h īkoi that nothing was set in stone. I bet that if he
had the opportunity to say a similar thing now, he would not use the word “stone”.
“Concrete” comes to mind in so far as Mr Hide is involved, because that man will not
be back. He has misled Auckland, he has di slocated the small num ber of supporters he
had there, and he has gone for popularity, wh ich has diminished. When that man comes
under pressure he refuses to step up to the plate and take responsibility, whether it
concerns overseas trips or Mr David Garrett. Now it is the M āori Statutory Board.
Rodney Hide was a key part of  the architecture group; he refuses to admit it, and he
refuses to accept any responsibility.
The person who is the most cunning of all in this, I have to say, is John Key. John
Key needs to keep sweet with the M āori Party in order to govern again. That is why he
is making only very mild remarks about the discredited M āori Statutory Board, which
does not have enough representatives from the great bulk of M āoridom in Auckland.
But wait! Help is on the way:  there will be two elected M āo ri representatives. We will
not have committees that are just adjuncts, which may actually cost a great deal of
money that is not transparently arrived at.
The board will pass slowly into history when we are in power and when our model
comes to pass, with two directly elected Māori representatives from the Māori roll. That
model was originally demolished by Warren Cooper, who was part of the dinosaur
discovery that emerged from the earth when the Christchurch earthquake spread further
down the South Island. One of his enduring features was to have tossed out that
particular innovation, which had been introduced in the time of David Lange. Help is on
the way for Māoris in Auckland.
The debate having concluded, the motion lapsed.
16838 Hamilton City Council (Parana Park) Land Vesting Bill 16 Feb 2011
HAMILTON CITY COUNCIL (PARANA PARK) LAND VESTING BILL
Second Reading
TIM MACINDOE (National—Hamilton West)  on behalf of David Bennett
(National—Hamilton East): I move, That the Hamilton City Council (Parana Park)
Land Vesting Bill be now read a second time. It is my great pleasure to open the second
reading of this debate on behalf of my colleague, the member for Hamilton East—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: I raise a point of order, Mr Speaker. I am doing this now in
the spirit of helpfulness rather than have the member start the speech all over again later
on. I think the member meant to say at the be ginning “On behalf of my colleague David
Bennett, I move,”. Otherwise, of course, he cannot move the motion.

items.speaker: The ASSISTANT SPEAKER
items.text: I guess that the member is technically
right. Speakers’ ruling 24/3 states “if the member … has the authority …”. Whether that
has to be stated is not something I have given consideration to, but it may be helpful if
the member just assures the House he has the authority.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: Thank you, Mr Assistant Speaker, and I thank the former
member for Hamilton West. On behalf of th e member for Hamilton East, I move that
the Hamilton City Council (Parana Park) Land Vesting Bill be now read a second time.
The city, and its representation, just gets bett er and better. It is my great pleasure to
open the second reading of this debate. Th e member for Hamilton East, as has been
noted by the former member for Hamilton West, is the sponsor of this bill, and Parana
Park is located in his electorate.
I believe we bring this legislation to the House with the full support of the Hamilton
City Council and, I think, the citizens of our fast-growing, diverse, and beautiful city.
Parana Park is located on the eastern side of the Waikato River in Hamilton, and
because that taonga marks the boundary betw een the electorates of Hamilton East and
Hamilton West, it is literally just a stone’s  throw from the constituency that I am
privileged to represent in this House—or, at  least, a stone’s throw for those who have a
better throwing arm than I do at the moment.

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: They shouldn’t throw stones.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: They throw peaches—they actually throw peaches on the river,
but that is another story. [ Interruption] I did not think this bill would be so
controversial. The purpose of this bill is to vest Parana Park in the Hamilton City
Council as a recreational reserve, subject to the provisions of the Reserves Act 1977.
The bill will repeal the Hamilton City (Parana Park) Empowering Act of 1958, which
was passed when Mr Mallard was in his mi ddle age and beginning his first campaign in
the electorate. Those of us whose children have grown up in or near Hamilton or who
are young enough, as Mr Mallard will be, to have childhood memories of playing in
Parana Park will know what a wonderful attr action it is for Hamiltonians. When my
children were little, they used to love playi ng in the park, especially on hot days, when
they would run in and out of the shallow pool or push their dolls and buggies while my
wife and I enjoyed our walks along the river path that wi nds through the park. It may
sound a little bit sentimental, but these memories linger in the minds of children and are
what great family memories are made of . My family has passed many happy hours in
Parana Park.

items.speaker: Grant Robertson
items.text: Tell us more about that.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: I know that Mr Robertson wa s also pushing his dolls and
buggies around in Parana Park many years ag o. It was always a pleasure to see him
there and we would welcome him back any time.
The area is equally well known now for its  civic importance, with poignant war
memorials; the cenotaph, which is the fo cal point of Anzac Day ceremonies; and an
16 Feb 2011 Hamilton City Council (Parana Park) Land Vesting Bill 16839
attractive park setting that is often used for public gatherings. The most recent of those
events, sadly, was a very moving memorial serv ice held last November, when the tragic
news that 29 lives had been lost in the Pike River mine disaster became known. That
was an occasion that I, and everybody present, will never forget.
Those are just some of the reasons why Para na Park is such a sp ecial feature of our
city, but it was not always available for its cu rrent purpose. The passage of this bill will
enable the Hamilton City Council to more effectively manage and administer Parana
Park. It will also enable the council to pro ceed with possible future development plans
for the area. The existing empowering Act does not make the area a reserve or provide
any special protection for Para na Park. It gives our counc il the power only to lease the
dwelling on the site and to allow other uses for it, because the council is constrained by
the provisions prescribed in the last will and testament of a great Hamiltonian, the late
George Parr.
The land now known as Parana Park, and its dwelling, was gifted in 1929 by Mr
Parr, a farmer and the son of a former mayor of the city, to be used for a children’s
convalescent home for patients from Waikato Hospital. About a quarter of a century
later it had become apparent that the house was not suitable for use as a convalescent
home, but as Mr Parr had wanted his propert y to be held as a children’s playground, the
decision was made that the council should manage it as a park for the benefit of local
citizens and visitors to Hamilton.
The 1958 empowering Act was passed by this  House under the guidance of one of
our greatest MPs, the late Dame Hilda Ross, to  facilitate that outcome. By that time the
paddling pool that I mentioned earlier and an  outdoor barbecue were  in frequent use,
and many trees had been planted to enhance the beauty of the ri verside setting. More
than half a century later the park is as beautiful and as popular as ever.
We are amazingly fortunate in our city not only to have a picturesque and well-used
park adjacent to the heart of our city but al so to boast what are arguably New Zealand’s
finest botanical gardens, within walking distance of Parana Park. I am sure many
members of this House have enjoyed visits  to the Hamilton Gardens and Parana Park,
and if any members have not, I invite them to do so because they are missing a treat. As
the annual Hamilton Gardens summer arts festival gets under way, I suggest that now is
the ideal time to plan that visit. The varied performances are always of an
extraordinarily high standard, and they are greatly enhanced by being held in such a
stunning setting. The finale, a sunset sy mphony performed by the Trust Waikato
Symphony Orchestra, attracts t housands of appreciative patrons and is always a world-
class crowd pleaser.
It is something of an indulgence to be ab le to stand in this  House and extol the
attractions and beauty of the delightful city of Hamilton. I am confident that members of
the House will welcome and support this measure, so I close by thanking members of
the Local Government and Environment Committ ee for their close consideration of this
bill.

items.speaker: Chris Auchinvole
items.text: It was a pleasure.

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: I thank Mr Auchinvole, and Dr Calder—two fine members. The
committee has reported the bill back with  some minor but worthy amendments
recommended, including an amendment to clause 6 to indicate that the reserve be
formally known as Parana Park, and to reinforce the fact that the Hamilton City Council
be the administering body of the reserve. I thank my colleague David Bennett for his
work in sponsoring this bill. On behalf  of our mayor, Julie Hardaker, our city
councillors, ratepayers, residents, and future generations—

items.speaker: Hon Trevor Mallard
items.text: Name them all—name the councillors; run through them.
16840 Hamilton City Council (Parana Park) Land Vesting Bill 16 Feb 2011

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: I could certainly do that. That member would like me to name
the councillors; I am happy to do that for him. He would remember many of them
well—people such as Peter Bos, Daphne Bell, Marijke Westphal, and Martin Gallagher
is one he would remember particularly well. I am delighted to see my predecessor there.
There is Gordon Chesterman, who is now the deputy mayor.

items.speaker: Chester Borrows
items.text: Chesterton—no relation to—

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: No, his name is Chesterman—not the great poet, but a great
man nevertheless. But I am aware of the fact that the whip is sitting here thinking that

items.speaker: TIM MACINDOE
items.text: I think I have done pretty we ll there. I thank all those
councillors. On behalf of the present and future generations of Hamilton, I thank all
